0.title: Vocation, Calling, and the Glory of God
0.essay:
Work is not a punishment, nor a necessary evil to be endured until the real business of life resumes on Sunday. It is a gift from a God who himself works.

A working God

Jesus said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). Work is rooted in the character of God. It was given to his image-bearers before the fall, it is redeemed by the gospel, and in transformed form it will continue into the new creation.

The Reformation’s gift

This was one of the Reformation’s most liberating insights, and one much of modern Christianity has forgotten. The medieval church drew a line between sacred and secular callings: monks, priests and nuns lived the truly holy life, while merchants, farmers and craftsmen were spiritually second-class. Luther shattered that line. Every lawful vocation, he insisted, is a calling from God, a place to love one’s neighbour and a place of real worship.

A saying often attributed to Luther puts it memorably: the Christian cobbler serves God not by putting little crosses on his shoes, but by making excellent shoes.

Work as discipleship

The working Christian is not a Christian who happens to work. They are a worker whose work is itself a form of discipleship: a daily arena where faith, love, integrity and the glory of God are all at stake.

The chapters

Created to Work: work before the fall. Work After the Fall: toil, frustration and grace. Vocation and Calling: every job as sacred calling. Work as Witness: the Christian in the workplace. Integrity and Excellence: work that honours God. And Rest and Sabbath: the rhythm that makes work sustainable and worshipful.

For reflection

Do you tend to think of your Monday work as part of your service to God, or as something separate from it?

1.title: Created to Work: Work Before the Fall
1.essay:
The first picture the Bible gives of God is a picture of a worker. “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).

God at work

Before there is a priest, a prophet or a king, there is a Creator. God speaks, forms, separates, gathers and makes. He brings order out of chaos and fullness out of emptiness. Then he looks at what he has made and calls it good. And then he rests, not from exhaustion but in the satisfaction of completed work. Work is a divine activity before it is a human one.

That is the foundation of work’s dignity. A person who works is not merely earning a living. At the deepest level, they are reflecting the image of the One who made them.

Work it and keep it

When God made humanity in his image, he immediately gave them work: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). Then “The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). The first word means to work, serve or till; the second, to keep, guard and preserve.

Adam was not placed in a leisure paradise. He was placed in a working garden. The garden was not finished; it was a beginning, with potential to develop. His task was to unfold that potential and extend its order, beauty and fruitfulness across creation.

Theologians call this the cultural mandate: the commission to take the raw material of creation and develop it into the fullness of human culture — agriculture, architecture, art, music, medicine, language, law. It is not a licence for exploitation but a call to stewardship. The scientist who studies creation, the artist who draws out its beauty, the farmer who cultivates its soil and the builder who shapes its materials into shelter are all, in their own domain, fulfilling this mandate.

Work and worship

The Hebrew word for “work” in Genesis 2:15 is the same word often used for worship and service to God. That is not a coincidence. Tending the garden was itself a form of service to God. A Christian whose work is done faithfully is not doing something pious alongside their work; their work itself becomes an act of worship.

Not a punishment

So work is not a consequence of the fall, but a gift of creation. The fall brought frustration and toil into work. It did not bring work itself. A Christian going to work on Monday morning is not leaving the sacred space of Sunday for the secular space of ordinary life. They are moving from one part of their calling to another.

Very good

“And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). This is the first quality assessment in history. It shows that work can be done well or poorly, and that there is a standard by which the difference is measured. The God who called his own work very good calls his image-bearers to excellent work. Craftsmanship, thoroughness and care are not perfectionism. They are the echo of the Creator in the creature.

Echoes of the Maker

To be made in God’s image is, among other things, to be made a worker and a maker. God creates; his image-bearers create. God orders and governs; so do they. The engineer who feels deep satisfaction when a bridge stands, the teacher whose student finally understands, the parent whose child flourishes — these are not accidental pleasures. They are echoes of what the Creator enjoyed when he looked at his finished work.

Dorothy Sayers, in her essay “Why Work?” (1942), argued that our creative impulse is one of the most godlike things about us. When someone makes something — a poem, a chair, a scientific discovery, a well-run household — they share in God’s creative activity. She lamented that the church had shrunk the gospel to personal salvation and left the working world to run on secular assumptions. The result was workers who felt their work was meaningless and their faith irrelevant to it.

Pray and work

The Benedictine tradition, following Benedict of Nursia, summed up its life in the motto ora et labora: pray and work. For Benedict, that rhythm was the shape of a holy life. The Reformation opened the insight to everyone. The monastery is not the only place where it applies. The marketplace, the classroom, the surgery and the kitchen are all places of prayer and work.

Still working

When Jesus healed on the Sabbath, he defended himself by saying the Father is still working. God did not stop after the creation week. He sustains, governs, redeems and renews. The Christian carries a remarkable truth into the workplace: the God who is still at work has called them to work alongside him, in their own domain, as his image and his representative.

For reflection

What has God given you to “work and keep” — in your job, your home or your community? Where do you feel the echo of the Maker’s satisfaction in your work?

2.title: Work After the Fall: Toil, Frustration, and Grace
2.essay:
The fall did not abolish work. It twisted it. Every working person knows the result, and the Bible is honest about it. But grace has entered the world of work too.

Thorns and thistles

Genesis describes the curse with painful precision. God told Adam, “cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:17–18). And “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground” (Genesis 3:19).

Notice that work itself is not cursed. The ground is. Work’s medium, the created world, becomes resistant. Its process becomes toilsome. Its outcome becomes uncertain. The goodness of work is not abolished, but obscured. That is why work can be satisfying and frustrating at the same time.

We know this in every field. The code that breaks. The client never satisfied. The crop that fails. The organisation that resists change. The colleague who undermines. The market that turns against years of planning. The body that tires. These are not merely bad luck or personal failure. They are the shape of work in a fallen world. The Christian names this honestly and does not pretend faith makes work easy.

Under the sun

Ecclesiastes is ruthlessly honest about work apart from God. “What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1:3). The Preacher worked harder, built more, planted more and gathered more than anyone, and found it all “vanity and a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11). He grieved that he must leave his wealth to someone who had not worked for it (Ecclesiastes 2:18–19).

He describes the exhausted worker exactly: “For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest” (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Anyone who lies awake running through today’s problems and tomorrow’s challenges knows what he means.

This is not cynicism. It is realism about what work can and cannot give. Work can give satisfaction, income, skill, community and contribution. It cannot give ultimate meaning, identity, security or salvation. Anyone who demands those from work will be as disappointed as the Preacher. His conclusion points to the true anchor: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

Common grace

Despite the fall, God sustains the created order and allows people to develop culture, discover truth, create beauty and build institutions that serve human flourishing. Theologians call this common grace: grace extended to all people, enabling even those who do not know God to do genuinely good work. Christians need not dismiss the work of unbelievers as worthless. They can recognise it as the fruit of God’s kindness and give thanks for it.

Christ’s world

The world in which we work is Christ’s world. “For by him all things were created,” Paul writes, and “in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17). That gives the physical creation a dignity that materialism cannot account for. The scientist studies what Christ holds together. The architect works with what he sustains. The farmer tends what he upholds. The Christian does not leave Christ behind at the church door on Sunday. They walk into a world that is, at its deepest level, his.

Not in vain

And grace does more. The gospel does not merely save souls and leave work to its distortions. It begins the redemption of work now and promises its completion in the new creation. Paul ends his great chapter on the resurrection with a word about work: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

The resurrection is the engine of that promise. Because Christ is risen, death has not had the final word over him, or over his people’s faithful work. How exactly faithful work is taken up into the new creation remains a mystery. That it is, Paul asserts with apostolic confidence. Work done in Christ — in faith, for God’s glory and in love of neighbour — carries a weight that outlasts its earthly form.

God milks the cows

Luther observed that in a fallen world even dull, tedious work is a form of love for neighbour. The farmer feeds his community even when farming is back-breaking and harvests uncertain. The mother who changes nappies serves her child even when the work is unglamorous and exhausting. Luther is often quoted as saying that God milks the cows through the farmer: the most ordinary work done faithfully is the instrument of God’s care for his people. That does not make the toil disappear. But it changes what the toil means.

For reflection

Where do you feel the thorns and thistles most in your work? What are you tempted to demand from work that only God can give? How does 1 Corinthians 15:58 speak to you?

3.title: Vocation and Calling: Every Job is Sacred
3.essay:
The word vocation comes from the Latin for “to call.” The Reformation recovered a simple and revolutionary truth: every Christian in every lawful occupation has been called by God.

Calling restored

The medieval church kept the language of calling for those who entered religious life. Monks, nuns and priests were called; everyone else merely worked. Luther overturned this. And the Gospels point the way. The eternal Son spent most of his earthly life in Nazareth, known as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). Those years were not wasted time but holy time, ordinary work sanctified by the presence of the Son of God. If he was pleased to work with his hands, no Christian need be ashamed of their trade.

General and particular callings

The Puritan William Perkins, in A Treatise of the Vocations (1603), taught that every believer has a general calling, as a Christian, and a particular calling, as a teacher, merchant, parent or magistrate. The particular calling is to be lived within the general one: as a Christian, for God’s glory, in love of neighbour. The quality and faithfulness of our daily work expresses how seriously we take our calling as Christians. A lazy or dishonest Christian worker is a contradiction in terms.

The life assigned

Paul writes, “Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (1 Corinthians 7:17). This is not fatalism. Paul allows for change when freedom comes (1 Corinthians 7:21). But his default is striking. The situation God has placed you in is not an accident to escape but a providential gift to inhabit faithfully. The first question is not “How do I get out of this?” but “How do I glorify God in this?”

That does not mean every job is equally fulfilling, or that God never calls people from one vocation to another. It means the question “Is God calling me into ministry?” must be answered not by assuming ministry is more sacred, but by honest discernment of gifts, opportunities and needs. The person who discerns they should stay in their trade is not settling for second best. They are answering a divine summons.

So that you may share

Paul tells the former thief, “Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28). The redeemed person is a working person, and work is redirected from taking what others have to producing what others need. That is the gospel’s transformation of work: from getting to giving, from accumulating to sharing.

Serving God by serving neighbour

Luther’s great insight, in effect, was that God does not need our good works, but our neighbour does. The motive for excellent work is not to impress God, who already accepts us in Christ, but to love the neighbour he places in our path through our work. The baker does not bake bread to earn grace. Grace is already given. She bakes good bread because her customers need it.

The Reformation’s recovery of the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9) applies here too. The teacher who serves her students, the nurse who cares for patients, the engineer who builds safe infrastructure: these are priestly acts, offering creation back to God through faithful stewardship.

Skill matters

“Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings” (Proverbs 22:29). The wisdom tradition honours excellence and skill as a real virtue. This is not just career advice. God cares about the quality of what his image-bearers produce, and developing skill is itself stewardship of the gifts he has given. Settling for mediocrity wastes what God entrusted.

The parable of the talents makes the same point. The master returns and says to the servants who invested and produced, “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much” (Matthew 25:21). Gifts are entrusted, not owned; they are given to be developed and used, not hoarded. One day the Master will ask what we did with what he gave us.

Discerning a calling

God’s calling to a particular work is usually discerned where three things meet: gifts (what can I do well?), opportunity (what doors has God opened?) and need (what does the world around me require?). Frederick Buechner put it memorably: vocation is where your deep gladness and the world’s deep hunger meet.

In the film Chariots of Fire, Eric Liddell says: “I believe God made me for a purpose, but he also made me fast. And when I run, I feel his pleasure.” Liddell did not treat running as a distraction from his “real” calling as a missionary to China. He treated it as a place where God’s glory was at stake, until God redirected him.

Tim Keller, in Every Good Endeavor, argues that work is not mainly about self-fulfilment or social impact, but about serving God and neighbour where he has placed you. The question is not “Does my work feel meaningful?” but “Am I doing this as to the Lord, in love of neighbour, for his glory?” A mundane job done that way is more sacred than a glamorous one done for self-promotion.

For reflection

Where do your gifts, your opportunities and the needs around you meet? Who is the neighbour your daily work serves, and how might seeing them change the way you work?

4.title: Work as Witness: The Christian in the Workplace
4.essay:
The workplace is one of the most significant mission fields in the world, and one of the most neglected. No church event gives an unbeliever the long, unfiltered view of the Christian life that a colleague gets over years.

Seen under pressure

Most Christians spend more waking hours at work than anywhere else. Colleagues know them over years, see them under pressure, and watch how they handle failure and success, disappointment and celebration. That is both an enormous opportunity and an enormous responsibility.

A Christian who is dishonest, lazy, complaining, scheming or contemptuous of colleagues is not merely failing professionally. They are damaging the reputation of the gospel. A Christian who is excellent, honest, generous, hardworking, kind under pressure and genuinely interested in colleagues’ flourishing is a living argument for the faith.

As for the Lord

“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:23–24). This is the most radical reframing of work in Scripture. Not just the overtly religious activities: whatever you do. At the desk, on your feet, behind the wheel, at the counter, in the operating theatre — you are serving the Lord Christ.

That changes both why and how we work. You are not performing for the boss or the appraisal. You are presenting your work to the Lord. Half-hearted work is not merely sloppy; it is a poor offering.

Adorning the gospel

Paul tells Christian slaves to be faithful and honest, “so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (Titus 2:10). The word adorn is the word for jewellery: to embellish, to make beautiful. A Christian’s conduct at work should not merely be inoffensive. It should make the gospel attractive. A colleague who sees a Christian behave badly concludes something about the faith that produced such behaviour. A colleague who sees a Christian show extraordinary grace under pressure may ask where it comes from.

Honourable conduct

Peter wrote to Christians living under suspicion in a pagan empire: “Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). Their defence was not first an argument, but a life. Live so honourably that the accusations have nowhere to land. This does not replace speaking about Christ. It earns that speaking the right to be heard.

Daniel in Babylon

Daniel and his friends were deported to Babylon, the most pagan empire of their world, and placed in the king’s service. They did not withdraw into a religious ghetto. They pursued excellence, and the king found them “ten times better” than all his magicians (Daniel 1:20). Yet they refused to compromise their convictions (Daniel 3:18; 6:10).

Decades later, Daniel’s jealous rivals searched his work for fault, “but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him” (Daniel 6:4). His only vulnerability was his devotion to God. That is the standard: a working life so excellent and honest that the only ground for attack is the faith itself. Most Christians face far less than Daniel did. But a Christian whose work and character cannot fairly be faulted leaves the watching world with one question: what makes this person different?

Relationships at work

The gospel transforms workplace relationships as well as work. Christians are to honour those in authority over them (1 Peter 2:18), to treat those under them with justice: “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1), and to pursue peace with everyone (Romans 12:18). In environments driven by self-advancement, that is countercultural. A Christian who celebrates colleagues’ successes without resentment, serves without manipulation, and speaks truthfully without cruelty is living out the gospel in one of the most visible places available.

The common good

The Christian worker works not only for themselves or their employer, but for the common good. The doctor who heals, the teacher who educates and the business that makes products meeting real needs all contribute to the flourishing God designed. Christians share that motive with many others, but they know its source: we serve our neighbours because God commands it and Christ showed it.

When work becomes a god

The workplace can easily become an idol: the source of identity, the measure of worth. When that happens, a Christian’s witness is compromised. They become indistinguishable from the driven, anxious culture around them. A person whose worth rests in Christ, not in a job title or performance review, has a freedom their colleagues do not. If your career is your god, losing it will devastate you. If the living God is your God, you can grieve a career loss and keep going. That freedom is itself a witness.

Stay where you are?

When William Wilberforce became a Christian, he considered leaving Parliament for the ministry. John Newton advised him to stay. Wilberforce took his political work as a calling from God and pursued it with extraordinary patience through some twenty years of defeats, until the slave trade was abolished. A Christian who asks, “Should I leave my job for ministry?” needs to hear Newton’s counsel: God may have placed you where you are precisely because he needs a faithful person there.

For reflection

What do your colleagues learn about Christ from watching you work? Where is one place this week where you could “adorn the doctrine of God” by the way you work or treat others?

5.title: Integrity and Excellence: Doing Work That Honours God
5.essay:
If our work is offered to the Lord, then its quality and honesty matter to him. Not because he accepts us on the basis of our performance, but because we are stewards who will one day give account.

Not justification, but stewardship

We are justified by faith alone, not by excellent quarterly reports. But a person given gifts, opportunities and a mandate to develop creation will answer for what they did with them. Integrity and excellence are not just professional virtues. They are acts of stewardship before God.

Integrity: no gap

Integrity means that what you are in private matches what you present in public. There is no gap between the face you show the boss, the face you show colleagues, and the person you are when no one is looking. For the Christian, this flows from knowing that someone is always looking. “I the LORD search the heart and test the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10).

The employee who works differently when the boss is out has a theology problem: they have forgotten that the Lord is always present. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10), and wisdom at work begins with remembering that our final accountability is not to the appraisal, the audit or the regulator, but to the One who sees everything.

Honest weights

The Old Testament is surprisingly specific about commercial honesty. “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). The word abomination is often used for idolatry. God takes commercial dishonesty as seriously as false worship, and he delights in fair dealing.

That reframes the thousand small choices of professional honesty: the accurate expense claim, the truthful product description, the fair price, the hours honestly worked. These are not only legal or professional matters. They are theological ones.

And the motive is grace. “You shall have just balances, just weights,” God told Israel, and then gave the reason: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:36). Those freely rescued from slavery owe honesty to their neighbours, not as payment for grace, but as its natural fruit. Christians, freely justified in Christ, are freed to deal honestly because they no longer need to grasp at security through commercial success.

Faithful stewards

Fiduciary duty — acting in the best interests of those who have entrusted their affairs to you — has deep biblical roots. Potiphar “left all that he had in Joseph’s charge” (Genesis 39:6). Jesus’ parables are full of faithful and unfaithful servants. Elders are entrusted with God’s flock (Acts 20:28). The Christian professional treats an employer’s resources, clients’ interests and colleagues’ wellbeing as sacred trusts.

George Müller, famous for his life of prayer, was also a man of remarkable financial integrity. He never went into debt, kept meticulous accounts, and published yearly reports of every gift received and spent. He believed the honesty of his finances was as much a witness to God’s faithfulness as the answered prayers. The God who provides does not need his servants to cut corners.

Excellence without anxiety

Excellence does not mean perfectionism or workaholism. It means bringing the best of your gifts and energy to the work in front of you — working with care, thoroughness and skill — and then leaving the outcome with God.

The excellent Christian worker is not driven by anxiety about results: am I good enough, will this work? They are driven by love for God and neighbour: I bring my best because the Lord deserves it and my neighbour needs it. That is a liberated excellence, freed from compulsive striving and grounded in the security of the gospel.

Lines we will not cross

There are things a Christian worker will not do, whatever the professional cost. Daniel would not eat the king’s food. His friends would not bow to the image. Peter and John would not stop preaching. A Christian asked to falsify data, misrepresent a product, undermine a colleague or betray a client must be ready to refuse, and to accept the consequences. Fear of God and fear of losing one’s job cannot both be the ultimate motive. Integrity sometimes costs, and it is wise to count that cost in advance.

The Christian who discovers serious wrongdoing in their organisation faces one of the hardest tests. Reporting it may cost their job, relationships and reputation. Ignoring it makes them complicit in the harm. The biblical framework is clear: God’s justice and the protection of neighbours come before professional self-preservation. But the decision needs wisdom, prayer, good counsel, and a willingness to suffer for doing right.

Suffering for doing good

“But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God” (1 Peter 2:20). The professional who loses a contract for refusing a bribe, a promotion for refusing to misrepresent, or a job for refusing to falsify, has not been abandoned by God. They are walking the path of the Servant who suffered for doing good and was vindicated in the resurrection. The commendation that matters does not come from the organisation. It comes from God.

For reflection

Is there any gap between who you are at work when watched and when unwatched? Where are the “honest weights” in your job? Is there a line you need to decide now that you will not cross?

6.title: Rest and Sabbath: The Rhythm That Redeems Work
6.essay:
Work without rest destroys the worker, and the witness the worker is meant to give. God built a rhythm into creation: work and rest, labour and delight.

God rested

God did not rest on the seventh day because he was tired. He rested to complete the rhythm of creation, to step back and enjoy what he had made, and to set the pattern his image-bearers would need in order to thrive. Rest is not an appendix to the working week. It is the frame that gives the week its meaning.

Two reasons to rest

The fourth commandment grounds Israel’s Sabbath in creation: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:9–10), for God rested on the seventh day. The version in Deuteronomy grounds it in redemption: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves cannot rest. Israel was no longer a slave.

Both reasons speak to Christians. We rest because we are made in the image of a God who rested, and because we have been freed from the slavery of sin and the tyranny of endless productivity.

Notice too that the commandment had two halves. Six days of work were commanded as well as one of rest. Many Christians feel guilty about failing to rest; fewer feel guilty about failing to work faithfully. Rest is the completion of labour, not an escape from it.

Fulfilled in Christ

The Christian’s relationship to the Sabbath is shaped by its fulfilment in Christ. “The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:28). Paul writes, “let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17).

So Israel’s weekly Sabbath law is fulfilled in Christ, and Christians are not bound to keep it as Israel did. But the rhythm of rest God built into creation remains a good gift, and the Lord’s Day gathers his people for worship. We do not rest to earn God’s favour. We rest because in Christ we already have it.

Rest for the soul

Jesus says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). He means more than physical rest. He means the soul’s rest in him. Many people are weighed down with the burden of earning their standing before God, proving their worth through achievement, carrying the anxiety of justifying themselves. Jesus invites them to lay it down.

“For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Not because the Christian life is effortless, but because the weight of justification has been lifted. A soul at rest in Christ’s acceptance can work with energy and joy instead of desperate striving.

A taste of the final rest

Hebrews sees the Sabbath as a picture of something greater: “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9–10). Each regular rest rehearses the final one. It is a small taste of the new creation, where there will be no more toil, no thorns and no thistles. The one who rests is not only resting. They are hoping.

The bread of anxious toil

“It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). The anxiety that drives overwork is, at root, a failure to trust God. The alternative is not laziness but trust: diligent work, followed by the sleep of someone who knows God is working while they sleep. For the Christian, even sleep is an act of faith.

Rest is trust

To stop is to declare that the world does not depend on my labour. The workaholic who cannot stop is, in effect, playing God, believing that everything hangs on their effort. Regular rest disciplines that belief out of us, training us week by week to trust the God who holds creation together.

In an age of smartphones, emails at midnight and constant availability, deliberate rest is one of the most countercultural and prophetic things a Christian can do. The Christian who is genuinely unavailable on their day off, who does not answer emails at midnight, preaches a sermon without words: there is a God who sustains this world, and I trust him enough to stop.

Rest for others

The fourth commandment explicitly included servants, animals and foreigners (Exodus 20:10). Rest was not a luxury for the powerful but a gift for everyone made in God’s image. A culture that denies rest to the vulnerable, through exploitative hours or the glorification of overwork, defies God’s design. Christians who seek fair working conditions for others are applying this principle in the public square.

Truett Cathy founded the restaurant chain Chick-fil-A and closed it every Sunday from the start, giving up enormous revenue so that his staff could rest and worship. He saw it as both faithfulness and a gift to his employees. The chain prospered anyway, and its Sunday closure remains a visible, costly declaration of its founder’s convictions.

Rest, play and worship

Rest is not a void to be filled with passive vegetation. It is a gift to be received with joy: worship with God’s people, enjoyment of creation — a long walk, a good meal, unhurried conversation — and simple delight in being alive rather than achieving. A person who rests well is a living parable of the rest that awaits the people of God.

For reflection

Do you rest in a way that expresses trust in God? What would it take for you to stop deliberately and regularly? Is there any “bread of anxious toil” you need to put down?
